newsitem.title: INDIA: India gold meeting highlights gold's uses - WGC.
newsitem.headline: India gold meeting highlights gold's uses - WGC.

text.p: Delegates to a global conference on gold on Friday called for steps to use the precious metal for the benefit of national economies, especially those of the developing countries.
Elliot Hood, chief executive of the World Gold Council (WGC), which organised the two-day conference, said the debate had helped dispel the traditional mystique around the subject.
"My principal conclusion would be that the conference has reduced the fear element about addressing issues to do with the gold market," Hood told Reuters in an interview soon after the meeting ended.
Hood said the notion that gold was a non-essential and non-priority item had substantially changed.
"Many speakers have clearly made the case that gold can be a vital, integral and useful part of a national economy and that there are a number of avenues to explore to make that happen," Hood said.
A case had been made economically and philosophically that gold could and should be an integral part of the Indian economy, he said.

India is the world's largest consumer of gold, using up an estimated 500 tonnes annually, most of which is imported. Official estimates put the cost of gold imports in calendar 1995 at $3.4 billion, next only to oil.

"Given that masses of India and the developing world have an implicit faith in gold, it is only fair that they should be allowed to do so at fair prices and use that asset to their own advantage," Hood said.
India's gold holdings are estimated at 9,016 tonnes, mainly accumulations from centuries of trading, and account for about 7.0 percent of an estimated world stocks of 128,800 tonnes.
Most of India's gold holdings comprise family heirlooms and dowry items accumulated over many years.
India could use its dormant gold resources to develop an export sector, Hood said.
"There is no reason, given India's infrastructure and its skills, that it should not be a major player in the gold export markets," he said.
Top officials of the Indian government who addressed the conference promised measures to boost gold's role in the national economy.
Commerce secretary Tejenra Khanna promised to allow higher imports of gold under special licences and to reduce customs duty on the metal.

India lifted a ban on gold imports in 1990 and gradually liberalised gold imports, allowing expatriate Indians to bring in up to five kgs of gold once every six months, subject to a duty of 220 rupees per 10 gm.
